claim: Synaptic currents display a large degree of heterogeneity of their temporal characteristics.
source: Synaptic currents display a large degree of heterogeneity of their temporal characteristics, but the functional role of such heterogeneities remains unknown.
evidence: This is stated as a premise in the abstract and is supported by the experimental data presented throughout the manuscript showing diverse temporal characteristics of UBC responses.

claim: UBCs respond to sinusoidal modulations of their sensory input with heterogeneous amplitudes and phase shifts.
source: We show that UBCs respond to sinusoidal modulations of their sensory input with heterogeneous amplitudes and phase shifts.
evidence: This claim is directly supported by experimental data shown in Figures 1, 2, and 4, demonstrating diverse phase shifts and amplitude responses across UBC populations.

claim: Phase inversion is produced by an mGluR2-activated outward conductance in OFF-UBCs.
source: While phase inversion is produced by an mGluR2-activated outward conductance in OFF-UBCs, the phase delay of ON UBCs is caused by a late rebound current resulting from AMPAR recovery from desensitization.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data in Figure 2 showing mGluR2-mediated currents and their correlation with phase shifts in OFF-UBCs.

claim: The phase delay of ON UBCs is caused by a late rebound current resulting from AMPAR recovery from desensitization.
source: While phase inversion is produced by an mGluR2-activated outward conductance in OFF-UBCs, the phase delay of ON UBCs is caused by a late rebound current resulting from AMPAR recovery from desensitization.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data in Figures 3 and 4 showing rebound currents and their correlation with phase delays, as well as cyclothiazide experiments blocking desensitization.

claim: Phase dispersion of UBC responses generates diverse phase coding in the granule cell population.
source: Granular layer network modeling indicates that phase dispersion of UBC responses generates diverse phase coding in the granule cell population, allowing climbing-fiber-driven Purkinje cell learning at arbitrary phases of the vestibular input.
evidence: This is supported by computational modeling results shown in Figure 6, demonstrating that networks with UBCs produce more diverse GC phase shifts than networks without UBCs.

claim: UBC phase diversity allows climbing-fiber-driven Purkinje cell learning at arbitrary phases of the vestibular input.
source: Granular layer network modeling indicates that phase dispersion of UBC responses generates diverse phase coding in the granule cell population, allowing climbing-fiber-driven Purkinje cell learning at arbitrary phases of the vestibular input.
evidence: This is supported by computational modeling results in Figure 7 showing that PCs can learn arbitrary phase relationships only in networks with UBCs.

claim: Primary vestibular neurons primarily encode the rotational velocity and linear acceleration of the head.
source: In the vestibular system, primary vestibular neurons primarily encode the rotational velocity (semicircular canals) and linear acceleration (gravitational or inertial, in the otholitic organs) of the head (Arenz et al., 2008; Fernandez and Goldberg, 1971; Goldberg, 2000; Goldberg and Fernandez, 1971a, 1971b; Green and Angelaki, 2010; Sadeghi et al., 2007).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to prior experimental work.

claim: The vestibulo-cerebellum is innervated by primary vestibular afferents in the vermal part.
source: The vestibulo-cerebellum, which is innervated by primary vestibular afferents in the vermal part (Barmack et al., 1993; Chabrol et al., 2015; Gerrits et al., 1989; Korte and Mugnaini, 1979) and by secondary vestibular afferents in all its subsections (Barmack et al., 1992; Magras and Voogd, 1985; Thunnissen et al., 1989), is well known to perform the sensory-motor integration required to orient the body in space and to generate accurate eye movements.
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to prior anatomical studies.

claim: The vestibulo-cerebellum is innervated by secondary vestibular afferents in all its subsections.
source: The vestibulo-cerebellum, which is innervated by primary vestibular afferents in the vermal part (Barmack et al., 1993; Chabrol et al., 2015; Gerrits et al., 1989; Korte and Mugnaini, 1979) and by secondary vestibular afferents in all its subsections (Barmack et al., 1992; Magras and Voogd, 1985; Thunnissen et al., 1989), is well known to perform the sensory-motor integration required to orient the body in space and to generate accurate eye movements.
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to prior anatomical studies.

claim: Primary vestibular mossy fibers activity displays a high level of stereotypy with mostly in-phase firing during sinusoidal velocity modulations.
source: In vivo electrophysiological recordings during passive head rotation indicate that primary vestibular mossy fibers activity displays a high level of stereotypy with mostly in-phase firing during sinusoidal velocity modulations (Arenz et al., 2008).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior in vivo electrophysiological work.

claim: Granule cells show a large diversity of phase shifts in response to head rotations in vivo.
source: Filtering may nevertheless occur upstream of granule cells, as the available in vivo recordings of granule cells show a large diversity of phase shifts in response to head rotations (Barmack and Yakhnitsa, 2008).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior in vivo recording studies.

claim: Each UBC receives a single mossy fiber input.
source: Each UBC receives a single mossy fiber input, and projects onto granule cells by forming several intrinsic mossy fiber terminals (iMFs).
evidence: This is established anatomical knowledge about UBC connectivity.

claim: UBCs project onto granule cells by forming several intrinsic mossy fiber terminals.
source: Each UBC receives a single mossy fiber input, and projects onto granule cells by forming several intrinsic mossy fiber terminals (iMFs).
evidence: This is established anatomical knowledge about UBC connectivity.

claim: The single mossy fiber contacting the dendritic brush of UBCs forms a giant synapse of unique morphology.
source: The single mossy fiber contacting the dendritic brush of UBCs forms a giant synapse of unique morphology (Mugnaini et al., 1994) at which various types of glutamate receptors are expressed (Jaarsma et al., 1995).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior anatomical studies.

claim: Various types of glutamate receptors are expressed at the MF-UBC synapse.
source: The single mossy fiber contacting the dendritic brush of UBCs forms a giant synapse of unique morphology (Mugnaini et al., 1994) at which various types of glutamate receptors are expressed (Jaarsma et al., 1995).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior molecular studies.

claim: Dorsal cochlear nucleus UBCs can be divided into ON UBCs and OFF UBCs.
source: In particular, Borges-Merjane and Trussell (2015) showed recently that dorsal cochlear nucleus UBCs can be divided into ON UBCs, which have an excitatory response to their mossy fiber inputs mediated by both AMPA and mGluR1 receptors, and into OFF UBCs, the response of which is inhibitory and is produced by mGluR2 receptor activation.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to a recent study by Borges-Merjane and Trussell (2015).

claim: ON UBCs have an excitatory response to their mossy fiber inputs mediated by both AMPA and mGluR1 receptors.
source: In particular, Borges-Merjane and Trussell (2015) showed recently that dorsal cochlear nucleus UBCs can be divided into ON UBCs, which have an excitatory response to their mossy fiber inputs mediated by both AMPA and mGluR1 receptors, and into OFF UBCs, the response of which is inhibitory and is produced by mGluR2 receptor activation.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Borges-Merjane and Trussell (2015).

claim: OFF UBCs have an inhibitory response produced by mGluR2 receptor activation.
source: In particular, Borges-Merjane and Trussell (2015) showed recently that dorsal cochlear nucleus UBCs can be divided into ON UBCs, which have an excitatory response to their mossy fiber inputs mediated by both AMPA and mGluR1 receptors, and into OFF UBCs, the response of which is inhibitory and is produced by mGluR2 receptor activation.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Borges-Merjane and Trussell (2015).

claim: Afferent vestibular inputs fire steadily at mean rates of 10–50 Hz at rest in vivo.
source: In vivo, afferent vestibular inputs fire steadily at mean rates of 10–50 Hz at rest (Arenz et al., 2008; Barmack and Yakhnitsa, 2008; Dickman et al., 1991; Fernandez and Goldberg, 1971; Goldberg, 2000; Goldberg and Fernandez, 1971a, 1971b; Green and Angelaki, 2010; Loe et al., 1973; Sadeghi et al., 2007; Tomko et al., 1981).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to prior in vivo recording studies.

claim: OFF-UBCs (n=25) were hyperpolarized by MF input at 26 Hz (−9.5 ± 4.2 mV at steady-state).
source: In a first group of cells (OFF-UBCs, n= 25, Figure 1A), the glutamatergic MF input evoked a hyperpolarization (−9.5 ± 4.2 mV at steady-state).
evidence: This claim is directly supported by experimental measurements reported in the text and shown in Figure 1A.

claim: In 5 OFF-UBCs, the hyperpolarization was preceded by a transient period of action potential firing (4 ± 2 spikes at 26.3 ± 15.2 Hz, duration 0.12 ± 0.06 s).
source: In 5 cells the hyperpolarization was preceded by a transient period of action potential firing (4 ± 2 spikes at 26.3 ± 15.2 Hz, duration 0.12 ± 0.06 s).
evidence: This claim is directly supported by experimental measurements.

claim: Out of 25 OFF-UBCs, 6 fired spontaneously (12.8 ± 8.1 Hz) at rest.
source: Out of 25 OFF-UBCs, 6 fired spontaneously (12.8 ± 8.1 Hz) at rest.
evidence: This claim is directly supported by experimental measurements.

claim: MF stimulation silenced 5 of 6 spontaneously firing OFF-UBCs and decreased firing rate by 28% in the last one.
source: MF stimulation silenced 5 of these UBCs and decreased firing rate by 28% in the last one.
evidence: This claim is directly supported by experimental observations.

claim: ON-UBCs covered a range of frequencies (1 – 29.9 Hz) similar to that found in vivo under anesthesia.
source: Overall, ON-UBCs covered a range of frequencies (1 – 29.9 Hz) similar to that found in vivo under anesthesia (Barmack and Yakhnitsa, 2008; Ruigrok et al., 2011; Simpson et al., 2005).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from this study and comparison to cited in vivo studies.

claim: Only 1 of 22 ON UBCs fired at rest (1.7 Hz) in the cell-attached configuration.
source: Only 1 of 22 ON UBCs fired at rest (1.7 Hz) in the cell-attached configuration.
evidence: This claim is directly supported by experimental observations.

claim: A group of complex UBCs (n = 10) displayed delayed or gradual depolarization which did not reach steady-state at the end of the MF stimulation protocol.
source: Finally, a group of complex UBCs (n = 10) displayed delayed or gradual depolarization which did not reach steady-state at the end of the MF stimulation protocol (Figure 1—source data 1A,E).
evidence: This claim is directly supported by experimental observations.

claim: 8 of 10 complex UBCs first hyperpolarized and then resumed firing at 10.9 ± 10.5 Hz with a delay from stimulation onset of 1.2 ± 1.3 s.
source: Similarly to OFF-UBCs, 8 of these 10 UBCs first hyperpolarized and then resumed firing at 10.9 ± 10.5 Hz with a delay from stimulation onset of 1.2 ± 1.3 s (from 0.44 to 4.16 s).
evidence: This claim is directly supported by experimental measurements.

claim: The slow inward current underlying the depolarization in complex UBCs was blocked by the group I mGluR antagonist JNJ16259685.
source: The slow inward current underlying the depolarization (Figure 1—source data 1B) was blocked by the group I mGluR antagonist JNJ16259685 (Figure 1—source data 1C).
evidence: This claim is directly supported by pharmacological experiments.

claim: The phase shift of ON-UBCs was broadly distributed (SD of 105°) and covered essentially all possible phase shifts.
source: The phase shift of ON-UBCs was broadly distributed (SD of 105°; Figure 1I) and covered essentially all possible phase shifts, with a sum of phase preferences weighted by the firing modulation strength of 140°.
evidence: This claim is directly supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1I.

claim: OFF-UBCs fired within a narrower range of phases (274 ± 28°) and had a significantly higher phase lag than ON-UBCs (p<0.001).
source: OFF-UBCs fired within a narrower range of phases (274 ± 28°; Figure 1D) and had a significantly higher phase lag than ON-UBCs (p<0.001; Figure 1J).
evidence: This claim is directly supported by experimental data and statistical analysis shown in Figures 1D and 1J.

claim: The firing modulation amplitude of OFF and ON cells was similar (12 ± 8 and 12 ± 23 Hz; respectively p=0.353).
source: The firing modulation amplitude of OFF and ON cells was similar (12 ± 8 and 12 ± 23 Hz; respectively p=0.353) but the dispersion of action potentials along the modulation cycle differed between these two populations.
evidence: This claim is directly supported by experimental measurements and statistical analysis.

claim: All UBCs (n = 21) responded to sinusoidal current injections at 1 Hz with a modest phase advance of 9.9 ± 4.1°, independently of the holding current bias.
source: We found that all UBCs (n = 21) responded with a modest phase advance of 9.9 ± 4.1° (Figure 1L), independently of the holding current bias, up to the sodium spike inactivation threshold (200 ± 85 pA).
evidence: This claim is directly supported by experimental measurements shown in Figure 1L.

claim: The sharpness of the UBC response to sinusoidal current injection was strongly regulated by the holding current, with hyperpolarized cells firing spikes concentrated at the peak of the sinusoidal current injection.
source: The sharpness of the UBC response was strongly regulated by the holding current, with hyperpolarized cells firing spikes concentrated at the peak of the sinusoidal current injection (Figure 1M).
evidence: This claim is directly supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1M.

claim: The strong heterogeneity in UBC phase shifts in response to MF stimulation is not due to intrinsic conductances.
source: Hence, the strong heterogeneity in UBC phase shifts in response to MF stimulation is not due to intrinsic conductances.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the experimental data showing minimal phase shifts with current injection compared to large phase shifts with synaptic stimulation.

claim: All OFF-UBCs displayed a slow outward post synaptic current that was blocked by the mGluR2 selective blocker LY341495.
source: All OFF-UBCs displayed a slow outward post synaptic current (PSC). This current was blocked by the mGluR2 selective blocker LY341495 (1 μM, n = 25, residual amplitude after block −5.3 ± 10.1 pA; Figure 2A).
evidence: This claim is directly supported by pharmacological experiments shown in Figure 2A.

claim: mGluR2 block revealed a NBQX-sensitive inward current in 48% of OFF-UBCs (n = 12) with peak 35.2 ± 28.7 pA.
source: mGluR2 block revealed a NBQX-sensitive inward current in 48% of OFF-UBCs (n = 12) (peak 35.2 ± 28.7 pA; NBQX block of the total charge 95 ± 9%; Figure 2B).
evidence: This claim is directly supported by pharmacological experiments shown in Figure 2B.

claim: The steady-state amplitude of mGluR2 PSC increased with the stimulation frequency from 10 Hz (41.5 ± 26.9 pA) to 100 Hz (129.9 ± 43.4 pA; n = 14 cells, p<0.001).
source: The steady-state amplitude of mGluR2 PSC increased with the stimulation frequency from 10 Hz (41.5 ± 26.9 pA) to 100 Hz (129.9 ± 43.4 pA; n = 14 cells, p<0.001) (Figures 2C and D).
evidence: This claim is directly supported by experimental measurements and statistical analysis shown in Figures 2C and D.

claim: The decay time constant of the mGluR2 EPSC was positively correlated with OFF-UBC phase shift (r = 0.621, n = 15, p<0.05).
source: OFF-UBC fired at the end of the period of low MF activity during 1 Hz modulations and their phase shift was positively correlated with the decay time constant of the mGluR2 current recorded in voltage-clamp (r = 0.621, n = 15, p<0.05) (Figure 2E).
evidence: This claim is directly supported by correlation analysis shown in Figure 2E.

claim: The total number of spikes per cycle in OFF-UBCs was positively correlated with the amplitude of mGluR2 hyperpolarization (r = 0.627, n = 18, p<0.01).
source: The total number of spikes per cycle was positively correlated with the amplitude of mGluR2 hyperpolarization (r = 0.627, n = 18, p<0.01), suggesting that rebound-promoting intrinsic conductances like IH or IT (Diana et al., 2007; Russo et al., 2007), amplify OFF-UBC responses.
evidence: This claim is directly supported by correlation analysis and inference about underlying mechanisms.

claim: The amplitude of OFF-UBC responses increased significantly from 0.3 Hz to 1 Hz and dropped at 3 Hz (p=0.0003; Friedman's test).
source: The amplitude of OFF-UBC responses increased significantly from 0.3 Hz to 1 Hz and dropped at 3 Hz (p=0.0003; Friedman's test; Figure 2H and I).
evidence: This claim is directly supported by experimental data and statistical analysis shown in Figures 2H and I.

claim: 20% and 68% of the OFF-UBCs were completely silenced during 1 Hz and 3 Hz modulations respectively.
source: Consistently with the increase of PSC amplitude at higher MF firing frequencies (Figure 2D), 20% and 68% of the OFF-UBCs were completely silenced during 1 Hz and 3 Hz modulationsrespectively (Figure 2H and 2I).
evidence: This claim is directly supported by experimental observations shown in Figures 2H and 2I.

claim: OFF-UBC phase shifts increased significantly with the modulation frequency (193 ± 46° at 0.3 Hz; 274 ± 28° at 1 Hz; 367 ± 29° at 3 Hz; p<0.0003; Friedman's test).
source: Phase shifts increased significantly with the modulation frequency (193 ± 46° at 0.3 Hz; 274 ± 28° at 1 Hz; 367 ± 29° at 3 Hz; p<0.0003; Friedman's test; Figure 2I).
evidence: This claim is directly supported by experimental data and statistical analysis shown in Figure 2I.

claim: In all ON-UBCs tested, EPSCs were blocked by the competitive AMPAR/kainate antagonist NBQX (block 92.6 ± 8.8% of the charge; n = 10).
source: In all ON-UBCs tested EPSCs were blocked by the competitive AMPAR/kainate antagonist NBQX (1 or 5 μM; block 92.6 ± 8.8% of the charge; n = 10; Figure 3A).
evidence: This claim is directly supported by pharmacological experiments shown in Figure 3A.

claim: The amplitude of the fast EPSC evoked by the first stimulation ranged from 5 to 210 pA (71 ± 66 pA; n = 21) and was inversely correlated to its decay time course (2.1 ± 1.5 ms) (r = 0.737; p<0.001; n = 21).
source: The amplitude of the fast EPSC evoked by the first stimulation ranged from 5 to 210 pA (71 ± 66 pA; n = 21) and was inversely correlated to its decay time course (2.1 ± 1.5 ms) (r = 0.737; p<0.001; n = 21; Figure 2—source data 1A).
evidence: This claim is directly supported by experimental measurements and correlation analysis.

claim: The amplitude of fast EPSCs decreased dramatically (by 67.4 ± 35.8% of the first peak at steady-state, n = 21) during 50 Hz trains.
source: Nevertheless the amplitude of fast EPSCs decreased dramatically (by 67.4 ± 35.8% of the first peak at steady-state, n = 21; Figure 3B), in a way which was inversely correlated to the decay time course of the first fast EPSC (r = 0.823; p<0.001; n = 21; Figure 3C).
evidence: This claim is directly supported by experimental measurements shown in Figure 3B.

claim: The decrease in fast EPSC amplitude during trains was inversely correlated to the decay time course of the first fast EPSC (r = 0.823; p<0.001; n = 21).
source: Nevertheless the amplitude of fast EPSCs decreased dramatically (by 67.4 ± 35.8% of the first peak at steady-state, n = 21; Figure 3B), in a way which was inversely correlated to the decay time course of the first fast EPSC (r = 0.823; p<0.001; n = 21; Figure 3C).
evidence: This claim is directly supported by correlation analysis shown in Figure 3C.

claim: Transient EPSCs were always accompanied by a low level of sustained steady AMPAR current (−15.9 ± 8.4 pA before the 4th stimulation).
source: Transient EPSCs were always accompanied by a low level of sustained steady AMPAR current (−15.9 ± 8.4 pA before the 4th stimulation; Figures 3A and B), indicative of the prolonged presence of glutamate in the synaptic cleft (Nielsen et al., 2004).
evidence: This claim is directly supported by experimental measurements shown in Figures 3A and B.

claim: In 67% of UBCs, an additional slow component developed during the train that reached a steady-state (64 ± 35 pA) with variable time course (τ = 0.347 ± 0.244 s at 50 Hz).
source: In 67% of UBCs, an additional slow component developed during the train, a further element suggesting glutamate concentration buildup in the synaptic cleft (Kinney et al., 1997). This slow EPSC buildup reached a steady-state (64 ± 35 pA; Figure 3D) with variable time course (τ = 0.347 ± 0.244 s at 50 Hz).
evidence: This claim is directly supported by experimental measurements shown in Figure 3D.

claim: The amplitude of the transient currents and of the buildup currents were not correlated (p=0.12).
source: The amplitude of the transient currents and of the buildup currents were not correlated (p=0.12; Figure 3E).
evidence: This claim is directly supported by statistical analysis shown in Figure 3E.

claim: In 87% of all AMPAR expressing UBCs (n = 27 out of 31 cells), an anomalous rebound current developed at the end of the stimulation.
source: In 87% of all AMPAR expressing UBCs (n = 27 out of 31 cells), an anomalous rebound current developed at the end of the stimulation (Figure 3A and B).
evidence: This claim is directly supported by experimental observations shown in Figures 3A and B.

claim: The amplitude of the rebound current (27.7 ± 16.7 pA) was correlated to its rise time constant (r = 0.583, p<0.01, n = 23).
source: The amplitude of the rebound current (27.7 ± 16.7 pA) was correlated to its rise time constant (r = 0.583, p<0.01, n = 23; Figure 3G), which varied widely from cell to cell (54 ± 24 ms; min = 25; max = 99; n = 23).
evidence: This claim is directly supported by correlation analysis shown in Figure 3G.

claim: The amplitude of the rebound current was correlated with both the amplitude of the transient EPSC integral (r = 0.611, p<0.01, n = 20) and with the amplitude of the slow buildup EPSC (r = 0.763, p<0.001, n = 25).
source: The amplitude of the rebound current was also correlated with both the amplitude of the transient EPSC integral (r = 0.611, p<0.01, n = 20; Figure 3H) and with the amplitude of the slow buildup EPSC (r = 0.763, p<0.001, n = 25; Figure 3I), suggesting that both fast and buildup components of transmission contribute to the genesis of the rebound.
evidence: This claim is directly supported by correlation analyses shown in Figures 3H and 3I.

claim: Cyclothiazide (10–20 µM) potentiated the charge during stimulation (201 ± 54% of control; n = 11) and suppressed the rebound current (27 ± 18% of control; n = 11).
source: Cyclothiazide (10–20 µM), a modulator of AMPARs known to suppress desensitization, potentiated the charge during stimulation (201 ± 54% of control; n = 11) and suppressed the rebound current (27 ± 18% of control; n = 11) (Figures 3J and K).
evidence: This claim is directly supported by pharmacological experiments shown in Figures 3J and K.

claim: The response phase of ON-UBCs at 1 Hz was linearly correlated with the ratio between the rebound charge and the synaptic charge during the 50 Hz trains (slope = 0.1 per 100°; r = 0.734, p<0.001, n = 22).
source: Indeed, the response phase of ON-UBCs at 1 Hz was linearly correlated with the ratio between the rebound charge and the synaptic charge during the 50 Hz trains (see Experimental Procedures) (slope = 0.1 per 100°; r = 0.734, p<0.001, n = 22; Figure 4D).
evidence: This claim is directly supported by correlation analysis shown in Figure 4D.

claim: In all delayed cells (positive phase shift), the phase of UBC firing was strongly correlated with the charge of the rebound EPSC (r = 0.75, p<0.001, n = 16).
source: In all delayed cells (positive phase shift), the phase of UBC firing was strongly correlated with the charge of the rebound EPSC (r = 0.75, p<0.001, n = 16; Figure 2—source data 1D).
evidence: This claim is directly supported by correlation analysis.

claim: The onset time constant of the rebound was strongly correlated to the phase of UBC firing (r = 0.87, p<0.001, n= 16).
source: Indeed we found that the onset time constant of the rebound was strongly correlated to the phase of UBC firing (r = 0.87, p<0.001, n= 16).
evidence: This claim is directly supported by correlation analysis.

claim: Cyclothiazide shifted the phase of UBC firing (143 ± 44° in control; −59 ± 36° in cyclothiazide; n = 7; p=0.01).
source: Cyclothiazide (Figure 4F), at a concentration which suppresses the rebound current, shifted the phase of UBC firing (143 ± 44° in control; −59 ± 36° in cyclothiazide; n = 7; p=0.01; Figure 4G) towards values similar to control cells displaying small rebound (p=0.9, n = 6 cells with little rebound current, n = 7 cells in cyclothiazide).
evidence: This claim is directly supported by pharmacological experiments and statistical analysis shown in Figures 4F and 4G.

claim: The average amplitude of ON-UBC firing modulation increased at higher MF modulation frequencies (5.1 ± 5.9 Hz at 0.3 Hz, 11.0 ± 8.1 Hz at 1 Hz, and 14.0 ± 9.7 Hz at 3 Hz; p=0.0009; Friedman's test).
source: In contrast to OFF-UBCs the average amplitude of firing modulation increased at higher MF modulation frequencies (5.1 ± 5.9 Hz at 0.3 Hz, 11.0 ± 8.1 Hz at 1 Hz, and 14.0 ± 9.7 Hz at 3 Hz; p=0.0009; Friedman's test).
evidence: This claim is directly supported by experimental data and statistical analysis.

claim: The population response of ON-UBCs showed significant frequency-dependent increase of phase lag (45.9° at 0.3 Hz, 108.9° at 1 Hz and 191.6° at 3 Hz; p<0.0001; Friedman's test).
source: The population response of UBCs also showed significant frequency-dependent increase of phase lag (45.9° at 0.3 Hz, 108.9° at 1 Hz and 191.6° at 3 Hz; p<0.0001; Friedman's test). and remained broadly distributed at all frequencies (SD: 76.3°, 73.9° and 92.7° at 0.3 Hz, 1 Hz and 3 Hz respectively; Figure 4I).
evidence: This claim is directly supported by experimental data and statistical analysis shown in Figure 4I.

claim: Phase dispersion of the ON-UBC responses is a property preserved over a wide range of movement dynamics.
source: Phase dispersion of the ON-UBC responses is therefore a property preserved over a wide range of movement dynamics.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the experimental data showing broad phase distributions at all tested frequencies.

claim: In most cells (14 out of 22) phase histograms of the simulated EPSCs and of the experimentally recorded UBC firing rate were significantly correlated (p<0.05; t-test).
source: In most cells (14 out of 22) phase histograms of the simulated EPSCs and of the experimentally recorded UBC firing rate were significantly correlated (p<0.05; t-test; Figure 5I).
evidence: This claim is directly supported by statistical analysis of model predictions versus experimental data shown in Figure 5I.

claim: Simulated and experimental phase shifts were linearly correlated (R = 0.89 and p=2e-5; t-test and slope = 1.04 for cells with correlated phase histograms).
source: Simulated and experimental phase shifts were linearly correlated (R = 0.89 and p=2e-5; t-test and slope = 1.04 for cells with correlated phase histograms) (Figure 5J).
evidence: This claim is directly supported by statistical analysis of model predictions versus experimental data shown in Figure 5J.

claim: The dynamics of glutamate accumulation at the MF to UBC synapse during time-modulated MF firing is the major determinant of firing phase in UBCs.
source: These data confirm that the dynamics of glutamate accumulation at the MF to UBC synapse during time-modulated MF firing is the major determinant of firing phase in UBCs.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the strong correlation between model predictions based on glutamate dynamics and experimental phase shifts.

claim: The distribution of phases in the network comprising UBCs is significantly closer to a uniform distribution compared to the network without UBCs (KS distance between network with UBCs and uniform: 0.1673; between network without UBCs and uniform: 0.4134; both distributions are significantly different, KS test, p<1e-10).
source: The distribution of phases in the network comprising UBCs is significantly closer to a uniform distribution compared to the network without UBCs (KS distance between network with UBCs and uniform: 0.1673; between network without UBCs and uniform: 0.4134; both distributions are significantly different, KS test, p<1e-10 (Figure 6Cii), similar to experimental in vivo data (Barmack and Yakhnitsa, 2008).
evidence: This claim is directly supported by statistical analysis of model simulations shown in Figure 6Cii.

claim: The heterogeneity of UBCs phase shifts leads to a diversity of GCs phase shifts.
source: Therefore, the heterogeneity of UBCs phase shifts leads to a diversity of GCs phase shifts.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the modeling results showing that networks with UBCs produce more diverse GC phase shifts.

claim: In a network with UBCs, the PC can learn to fire at arbitrary target phases.
source: Figure 7 shows that in a network with UBCs, the PC can learn to fire at arbitrary target phases, even though eMF inputs peak only at two possible phases (Figure 7A, top and Figure 7B).
evidence: This claim is directly supported by modeling results shown in Figure 7.

claim: In a network without UBCs, PCs can only learn to fire in phase with eMF inputs.
source: This ability breaks down in a network without UBCs, in which PCs can only learn to fire in phase with eMF inputs (Figure 7A, bottom and Figure 7B).
evidence: This claim is directly supported by modeling results shown in Figure 7.

claim: UBCs in the vestibular cerebellum behave as a bank of diverse temporal filters.
source: Our study reveals that populations of UBCs in the vestibular cerebellum behave as a bank of diverse temporal filters.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the experimental data showing diverse temporal response properties across the UBC population.

claim: The UBC extends the combinatorial notions of pattern separation and expansion recoding into the temporal domain.
source: The UBC therefore extends the combinatorial notions of pattern separation (Marr, 1969) and expansion recoding (Albus, 1971) into the temporal domain.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the experimental and modeling results, drawing on established theoretical concepts.

claim: The diversity of UBC responses is due to a combination of heterogeneous expression of ionotropic and metabotropic glutamate receptors and the variability of AMPAR-mediated responses.
source: We have established that the diversity of UBC responses is due to a combination of two factors: (1) the heterogeneous expression of ionotropic and metabotropic glutamate receptors (see also Borges-Merjane and Trussell, 2015) and (2) the variability of AMPAR-mediated responses, due to cell-specific combinations of transient, build-up and rebound synaptic components.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the experimental data showing different receptor types and synaptic response profiles across UBCs.

claim: The paucity of ionotropic receptors at some mGluR2-expressing MF-UBC synapses is surprising, given the size of the synaptic articulation and the number of synaptic release sites.
source: The paucity of ionotropic receptors at some mGluR2-expressing MF-UBC synapses is also surprising, given the size of the synaptic articulation and the number of synaptic release sites (Mugnaini et al., 1994).
evidence: This claim is inferred from the experimental observations of OFF-UBCs with dominant mGluR2 responses and minimal AMPAR currents.

claim: The predominance of mGluR transmission at the MF synapse is not directly linked to the giant synaptic articulation, as mGluRs are exclusively found at extrasynaptic sites on the dendritic appendages of the UBC brush.
source: The predominance of mGluR transmission at the MF synapse is not directly linked to the giant synaptic articulation, as mGluRs are exclusively found at extrasynaptic sites on the dendritic appendages of the UBC brush (Jaarsma et al., 1998).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior anatomical studies.

claim: To account for late-phase responses and for the wide bandwidth of UBC modulations, the AMPAR must present a bell-shaped steady-state response curve.
source: To account for late-phase responses and for the wide bandwidth of UBC modulations, the AMPAR must present a bell-shaped steady-state response curve, as described experimentally (Kinney et al., 1997).
evidence: This claim is inferred from modeling results and supported by citation to prior experimental work.

claim: The combination of bell-shaped steady-state AMPAR response and spillover-induced desensitization at the UBC synapse generates strong rebound currents following a train of MF action potentials.
source: The combination of these properties and of spillover-induced desensitization at the UBC synapse generates strong rebound currents following a train of MF action potential (see also van Dorp and de Zeeuw, 2014).
evidence: This claim is inferred from experimental observations and modeling results.

claim: A combination of factors, including the complex geometry of MF-UBCs synapse, the variety of AMPARs and auxiliary subunits, and the localization of AMPARs with respect to release sites, could explain the variety of AMPA EPSCs profiles at MF to UBC synapses.
source: We hypothesize that a combination of factors, including the complex geometry of MF-UBCs synapse, the variety of AMPARs and auxiliary subunits (Jackson and Nicoll, 2011), and the localization of AMPARs with respect to release sites (Jaarsma et al., 1995), could explain the variety of AMPA EPSCs profiles at MF to UBC synapses.
evidence: This is a speculative hypothesis based on inference from experimental data and cited literature.

claim: The desensitized states are important for the functional properties of ionotropic glutamate receptors.
source: Our results strongly support the importance of the desensitized states for the functional properties of ionotropic glutamate receptors.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the experimental data showing the role of desensitization in generating rebound currents and phase delays.

claim: UBCs can generate much larger delays than other sources of diversity in phase responses, as well as OFF-responses, within a wide range of stimulation frequencies.
source: However, we showed here that UBCs can generate much larger delays, as well as OFF-responses, within a wide range of stimulation frequencies.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the experimental data showing large phase shifts in UBCs compared to other reported mechanisms.

claim: The variable tuning frequency of UBCs could explain the frequency-specific learning of the VOR gain modulation.
source: The variable tuning frequency of UBCs could explain the frequency-specific learning of the VOR gain modulation (Lisberger et al., 1983), because different populations of UBCs and hence of granule cells would be optimally modulated for different rotation frequencies.
evidence: This is a speculative hypothesis based on inference from experimental data and cited literature.

claim: UBCs have the capability to generate high-frequency rebound bursts, which may provide useful timing information.
source: Finally UBCs have the capability to generate high-frequency rebound bursts (Diana et al., 2007; Locatelli et al., 2013), as shown here for some of the OFF-UBCs, which may provide useful timing information, as suggested in the electro-sensory lobe of the electric fish (Kennedy et al., 2014; Sawtell, 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from this study and citations to prior work.

claim: Golgi cell inhibitory inputs to UBCs may enhance rebound behavior.
source: Golgi cell inhibitory inputs to UBCs (Dugue et al., 2005), which were pharmacologically blocked in this study, may enhance this rebound behavior (Kennedy et al., 2014), providing for richer interactions between the granular layer dynamics and UBC intrinsic excitability.
evidence: This is a speculative hypothesis based on inference and cited literature.

claim: UBCs play a preferential role in tasks in which non trivial associations between inputs and outputs at different phases need to be learned.
source: Our data support a preferential role of UBCs in tasks in which non trivial associations between inputs and outputs at different phases need to be learned, like phase-shifted VOR or high-velocity compensatory eye movements during which non-linear inverse eye dynamics have to be computed (Green et al., 2007; Lisberger, 2009).
evidence: This claim is inferred from the experimental and modeling results, supported by citations to relevant motor control literature.

claim: Optogenetic suppression of vestibular UBC activity should lead to significant impairment in motor tasks requiring phase-specific learning.
source: Optogenetic suppression of vestibular UBC activity should lead to significant impairment in these motor tasks.
evidence: This is a speculative prediction based on inference from the experimental and modeling results.

claim: The higher prevalence of UBCs in the hemispheric lobules in higher mammals argues for the involvement of this cell-type in complex motor and cognitive tasks involving the cerebellum.
source: Furthermore the higher prevalence of UBCs in the hemispheric lobules in higher mammals (Dino et al., 1999) argues for the involvement of this cell-type in complex motor and cognitive tasks involving the cerebellum.
evidence: This claim is inferred from anatomical observations cited from prior work.
